$scopeNote: Only ORDINARY (consumer/creditor judgment) wage garnishment is state-overridable here. Federal law — support orders, federal tax levies, federal student loan default — preempts a state's own wage-exemption statute entirely, so nothing in this file ever changes those two calculations in src/garnishment.ts; only 'consumer_creditor' orders consult it. A state absent from this file has no known departure from the plain federal CCPA default and is computed with it as-is — a narrower claim than 'every state's garnishment law has been fully researched.' Only a handful of states are covered: the ones with a clean, well-documented, easily-verified departure (an outright statutory prohibition, or a materially different percentage/floor formula). Most states track the federal default exactly or vary it only at the margins (a lower percentage for very low earners, a different priority-of-orders rule) that this pass didn't chase down — same disclosure discipline as this project's data/states/*.json knownGaps.

NC.knownGap: Some secondary sources frame this as North Carolina simply not providing attachment as a creditor remedy against a resident's wages at all (rather than a bare percentage exemption); this file only asserts the practical outcome relevant to this engine — an ordinary consumer_creditor garnishment computes to $0 in NC — not the precise doctrinal mechanism.

IL.$note: Unlike every other figure in this file, Illinois's OWN minimum wage — not the federal $7.25 figure the rest of this file and federal-2026.json use — drives the 45x floor, because 735 ILCS 5/12-803 takes the GREATER of the two and Illinois's has been higher since 2022. The 15% fraction here applies to GROSS wages, not disposable earnings, which is why this state carries its own maxGrossEarningsFraction field instead of reusing maxDisposableEarningsFraction. Re-verify stateMinimumHourlyWage every year this file rolls forward — it is not sourced from anywhere else this engine already tracks.
